claim: Docs say CLAUDE.md should stay under 200 lines, and growing reference content should move to skills or to path-scoped .claude/rules files.
why: CLAUDE.md loads in full every session, so every line costs context on every request.
check: Count lines in each loaded CLAUDE.md; over 200 lines, or containing reference material (API docs, long procedures), is a finding.
quote: Keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines. If it's growing, move reference content to skills or split into

claim: Guardrails that must always hold belong in hooks, not in CLAUDE.md or skill text, because an instruction there is a request rather than a guarantee.
why: A PreToolUse hook blocks the action regardless of what the model decides; prose instructions are only followed by judgment.
check: Look for 'never X' or 'always Y' lines in CLAUDE.md or skills that guard something critical (secrets, migrations, generated code) with no hook or deny rule behind them.
quote: An instruction like "never edit `.env`" in CLAUDE.md or a skill is a request, not a guarantee.

claim: The docs' hook-vs-skill table says a hook fires on its lifecycle event without Claude deciding, while a skill is instructions Claude interprets so outcomes can vary.
why: Determinism is the deciding axis: use hooks for fixed mechanical actions, skills for work that needs reasoning.
check: Flag skills that are really fixed scripts (format, lint, notify) that should be hooks, and hooks that try to encode judgment.
quote: Fires on its event without Claude deciding

claim: A hook costs zero context unless it returns output, while a skill's description loads every session and its full content loads when used.
why: Loading strategy differs per extension point and drives context cost.
check: Check hooks that print verbose stdout or additionalContext on every event, since that output becomes conversation context.
quote: Zero unless the hook returns output

claim: CLAUDE.md and output styles are both standing instructions that Claude follows as instructions, so neither is enforced; output style carries role/tone/format, CLAUDE.md carries project facts and rules.
why: They combine: CLAUDE.md stays loaded whichever style is active, and enforcement needs a hook.
check: Flag CLAUDE.md lines about response length, tone, or persona that belong in an output style, and style files that hold project facts.
quote: Claude follows both as instructions, so neither is enforced.

claim: MCP gives Claude tools and data access to an external system; a skill gives it knowledge about how to use those tools well; the docs treat them as complementary, not alternatives.
why: They solve different problems: connectivity versus know-how.
check: Flag skills that try to reach external systems by pasted credentials or ad hoc curl where an MCP server fits, and MCP servers whose usage conventions are undocumented.
quote: MCP connects Claude to external services. Skills extend what Claude knows, including how to use those services effectively.

claim: Skill vs subagent: a skill adds content to the main context window, while a subagent runs in a separate window with its own input and output tokens and returns a summary.
why: Choose a subagent for context isolation, parallel or specialized work; choose a skill for reusable reference or invocable workflows.
check: Flag subagents used merely to hold reference text (a skill fits), and skills that make the main thread read dozens of files (a subagent fits).
quote: Uses a separate window with its own input and output tokens

claim: Dynamic workflows are for jobs that outgrow a handful of subagents or need findings cross-checked, with a script deciding what runs next; subagents are for quick focused workers where Claude decides turn by turn.
why: The docs distinguish who controls sequencing: Claude per turn versus a script.
check: Flag setups that hand-orchestrate many subagents from CLAUDE.md prose where a saved workflow would be deterministic.
quote: With subagents, Claude decides turn by turn what runs next. In a workflow, the script decides:

claim: A plugin is the packaging layer that bundles skills, hooks, subagents, and MCP servers into one installable unit, for reuse across repositories or distribution via a marketplace.
why: Plugins do not add a new kind of capability; they distribute existing ones.
check: A plugin holding only one trivial file, or a setup copy-pasted across repos instead of packaged, is a finding.
quote: A plugin bundles skills, hooks, subagents, and MCP servers into a single installable unit.

claim: Plugin skills are namespaced like /my-plugin:review so several plugins can coexist without name collisions.
why: Plain skills override by name across levels, so namespacing avoids clashes.
check: When two plugins or a plugin and a project skill share a bare name, check which one resolves.
quote: Plugin skills are namespaced (like `/my-plugin:review`) so multiple plugins can coexist.

claim: When the same name exists at several levels, skills and subagents override by name (skills: managed > user > project; subagents: managed > CLI flag > project > user > plugin), MCP servers override local > project > user, CLAUDE.md files are additive, and hooks all fire.
why: Different extension points layer differently, so a duplicate can silently shadow or stack.
check: Look for same-named skills/agents/MCP servers at multiple scopes, and for hooks registered in several sources that both fire.
quote: when the same name exists at multiple levels, one definition wins based on priority (managed > user > project for skills; managed > CLI flag > project > user > plugin for subagents)

claim: When CLAUDE.md files at different levels conflict, Claude uses judgment to reconcile them rather than applying a deterministic precedence.
why: CLAUDE.md is additive context, not a override chain.
check: Check user, project, and subdirectory CLAUDE.md for contradictory instructions.
quote: When instructions conflict, Claude uses judgment to reconcile them.

claim: All registered hooks fire for a matching event regardless of whether they come from user, project, plugin, or managed sources.
why: Hooks merge across sources instead of overriding by name.
check: Run /hooks and look for duplicated hooks from several sources that double-run a formatter or notifier.
quote: all registered hooks fire for their matching events regardless of source

claim: Context cost differs by feature: CLAUDE.md and output styles cost every request, skills cost descriptions every request with full content on use, MCP costs tool names with schemas deferred, subagents are isolated, hooks are free unless they return output.
why: The docs warn that too many extensions fill the window and add noise that makes skills mis-trigger and conventions get lost.
check: Total the always-loaded parts (CLAUDE.md, output style, skill descriptions, MCP server instructions) and compare to the work done.
quote: Every feature you add consumes some of Claude's context.

claim: With disable-model-invocation: true a skill's description stays out of context entirely and it runs only when the user names it; the docs recommend this for skills with side effects.
why: It saves context and prevents Claude from starting the skill on its own.
check: Flag deploy/release/delete-style skills that lack disable-model-invocation, and rarely used manual skills that still spend description tokens.
quote: Use `disable-model-invocation: true` for skills with side effects. This saves context and ensures they run only when you name them.

claim: Claude picks skills by matching the task against names and descriptions, so vague or overlapping descriptions cause the wrong skill to load or a useful one to be missed.
why: Description is the only routing signal before the full content loads.
check: Review skill descriptions for vagueness or overlap between skills.
quote: If descriptions are vague or overlap, Claude may load the wrong skill or miss one that would help.

claim: A custom subagent starts with its own system prompt, not the Claude Code system prompt, and the built-in Explore and Plan agents skip CLAUDE.md at startup.
why: Subagent context is isolated, so project rules do not automatically reach every worker.
check: If a rule must bind Explore/Plan, it must be restated in the delegating prompt; for custom subagents, critical rules belong in the agent file body.
quote: The agent's own system prompt, not the Claude Code system prompt

claim: The built-in Explore and Plan agents skip CLAUDE.md at startup, so instructions in CLAUDE.md will not reach them.
why: The debug table lists this as a cause of 'subagent ignores CLAUDE.md'.
check: If a setup relies on CLAUDE.md to steer search or planning subagents, verify the instruction is passed in the delegating prompt.
quote: The built-in Explore and Plan agents skip `CLAUDE.md` at startup.

claim: The docs list the triggers for adding each extension: a repeated mistake goes to CLAUDE.md, a repeated prompt or playbook to a skill, an inaccessible system to MCP, an every-time need to a hook, and a second repo needing the same setup to a plugin.
why: Setups should grow from observed triggers, not be configured up front.
check: Flag speculative extensions with no recurring trigger behind them.
quote: A repeated mistake or a recurring review comment is a CLAUDE.md edit, not a one-off correction in chat.

claim: Output styles are the intended place for response voice, length, format, or a non-engineering role, switchable one at a time.
why: It is the one extension scoped to how Claude responds rather than what it knows.
check: Flag CLAUDE.md sections about tone, verbosity or format that should be a style you can toggle off.
quote: A voice, length, or format you want in every response, or Claude working as something other than a software engineer

claim: Path-scoped rules (.claude/rules with a paths: filter) load only when Claude works on matching files, so language- or directory-specific guidance should live there instead of in CLAUDE.md.
why: This keeps CLAUDE.md focused and saves context.
check: Flag CLAUDE.md sections about one subsystem or language that could be a rule with paths:.
quote: with a `paths:` filter so it only loads when Claude is actually working there

claim: Per-directory CLAUDE.md fits when directory owners maintain conventions versioned with the code; a central path-scoped rule fits when you want all conventions in one place or one rule spans scattered paths.
why: The two differ in location and in when they load.
check: In monorepos, see whether subsystem conventions sit in the right one of these and are not duplicated at the root.
quote: You want all conventions in one place, or the same rule applies to many scattered paths

claim: Only write down in CLAUDE.md what Claude cannot find by reading the repo or would otherwise spend time rediscovering every session.
why: Current models read the repo very well, and each CLAUDE.md line takes attention on every task.
check: Flag CLAUDE.md content describing file layout, framework choice, or conventions evident from code.
quote: Only write down what Claude can't find by reading the repo, or what it would otherwise spend time rediscovering every session.

claim: Docs say a good CLAUDE.md holds the exact test, typecheck, and lint commands including running a single test, misleading places in the code, decisions not in the repo, and anything corrected twice.
why: These are what Claude cannot infer from code and needs to verify its own work.
check: A CLAUDE.md with no verification commands, or full of architecture descriptions, is a gap.
quote: How to confirm work in this repo: the exact test, typecheck, and lint commands, and how to run a single test file

claim: The current docs list 'describe your architecture and file layout in CLAUDE.md' as advice to stop following.
why: Claude reads the repo itself, so such text is redundant context.
check: Flag architecture overviews and directory trees in CLAUDE.md.
quote: Claude reads the repo itself. Only write down what isn't in there.

claim: If Claude keeps missing a CLAUDE.md line, adding emphasis is the wrong fix: either shorten the file or turn a no-exceptions rule into a hook.
why: Current models follow plain wording, and piling on emphasis makes them over-apply the rule.
check: Flag IMPORTANT/ALL CAPS/NEVER emphasis in instruction files.
quote: piling on emphasis mostly makes Claude over-apply the rule

claim: Hooks should be reserved for rules with zero exceptions; preferences stay in CLAUDE.md, and hooks that only encode preferences should be deleted.
why: Every hook and deny rule will occasionally misfire and has to be maintained.
check: Count hooks and deny rules; around forty is the docs' signal that most are preferences.
quote: If you ever find yourself at forty of them, most are probably preferences that Claude could have weighed on its own.

claim: prompt and agent hooks ask another model to decide, so they are not deterministic; real enforcement needs command or http hooks, plus onFailure: block if a crashed hook must also stop the action.
why: A model-judged hook can be wrong, and a failing scanner would otherwise let the action through.
check: Check security-critical hooks for type prompt/agent, and whether onFailure is set where fail-open is unacceptable.
quote: so it isn't deterministic either. For real enforcement, use a `command` or `http` hook

claim: Deny permission rules hold in every permission mode including auto and bypassPermissions, which makes them the right place for never-read rules like .env.
why: Deny and ask rules and PreToolUse hooks run before the auto-mode classifier.
check: Check that secrets and protected paths are in permissions.deny, not only in CLAUDE.md.
quote: `deny` rules hold in every permission mode, including auto and `bypassPermissions`

claim: A WebFetch domain deny rule does not stop curl to that domain unless the sandbox is on, and a Read deny rule does not catch a script that opens the file.
why: Rules match tool calls, not intent.
check: For security boundaries, check that the sandbox is enabled alongside the permission rules.
quote: A `WebFetch` deny rule for a domain does nothing about `curl` to that same domain, unless the sandbox is on.

claim: Bash deny rules match the literal command string, not the underlying executable, so Bash(rm *) does not block /bin/rm or find -delete; use a PreToolUse hook or the sandbox for a hard guarantee.
why: Command-text matching can be sidestepped by an equivalent form.
check: Review Bash deny rules for protection that relies on string patterns only.
quote: Bash rules match the literal command string, not the underlying executable

claim: Auto mode is a classifier model judging actions, not a hard rule, so never-rules belong in deny rules or hooks; a sentence in the conversation can also be lost at compaction.
why: It can be wrong, can be tuned, and can be disabled by the organization.
check: Check that safety-critical prohibitions are not left to auto mode or conversation text.
quote: Auto mode is a classifier model judging each action rather than a hard rule.

claim: In autoMode settings every list should keep "$defaults", otherwise entries replace the built-in rules, and the autoMode block must be in user settings because the classifier ignores project autoMode.
why: Without $defaults a soft_deny list drops the built-in blocks on force pushes and production deploys.
check: Inspect autoMode in settings for a missing $defaults or a project-level autoMode block.
quote: The `autoMode` block also has to live in `~/.claude/settings.json` rather than the project, because the classifier ignores `autoMode` in project settings.

claim: A Stop hook that exits with code 2 sends stderr back to Claude and forces more work, but Claude Code overrides after 8 consecutive blocks by default.
why: The cap prevents infinite loops; CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP raises it and 0 disables it.
check: Check Stop hooks for a way to terminate (the check eventually passes) and for stderr redirection of the output.
quote: (default: 8). Set to `0` to disable the cap.

claim: Give Claude a pass/fail check it can run (tests, typecheck, linter, build exit code, screenshot); the docs call the command that runs it the most useful line in CLAUDE.md.
why: Claude stops when work looks done, and without a check the user becomes the test suite.
check: Look for a verification command in CLAUDE.md or a Stop hook; absence is a finding.
quote: Claude stops when the work looks done.

claim: Verification strictness ranges from a prompt request, to /goal (a separate model checks a condition each turn), to a Stop hook (harness-enforced), to a fresh-subagent /code-review; the docs recommend asking Claude for evidence, not just a claim of success.
why: An unattended run's evidence is the only record of what happened.
check: For unattended or long runs, check that a goal or Stop hook exists and the prompt asks for command output.
quote: "All tests pass" on its own tells you very little, and reading the output is faster than rerunning the check yourself.

claim: When asking a subagent to review against a spec, tell it to skip style and report only correctness gaps.
why: A reviewer asked to find problems will always find something, and fixing every finding adds abstraction and tests for impossible cases.
check: Review prompts and reviewer agents for an unbounded 'find issues' instruction.
quote: If you fix every finding, you end up with extra abstraction layers and tests for cases that can't happen.

claim: Restricting a custom subagent to tools: Read, Grep, Glob makes a read-only reviewer whose limit is enforced by Claude Code rather than requested in a prompt.
why: Tool allowlists are deterministic; prompt restrictions are not.
check: Reviewer or research agents that inherit all tools should usually be narrowed.
quote: that limit is enforced by Claude Code rather than requested in a prompt.

claim: Subagents cost mostly tokens, since each sends its own requests against the same usage, can be slower than doing the task in place, and give parallelism or a fresh reviewer but not a smarter answer.
why: A fresh subagent must re-gather context the conversation already has.
check: Flag setups that delegate small tasks to subagents by default or expect delegation to improve quality.
quote: What they cost you is mostly tokens, since every subagent sends its own requests and they count against the same usage as your main conversation.

claim: Use model: haiku in the definition of subagents doing simple jobs (collecting importers, checking links), and ask for short summaries back.
why: Haiku costs much less per request and simple jobs do not need the larger model.
check: Check cheap-looking subagents for an unset or expensive model.
quote: Haiku is a good fit for subagents doing simple jobs.

claim: Within the docs, the best-practices page says 'use subagents to protect your context window' is outdated advice, while the features overview still says to use a subagent when the context window is getting full.
why: The two official pages weigh the context-isolation benefit differently; best practices says running out of context is now rare and each subagent costs extra tokens.
check: Do not penalize a setup for using subagents for isolation, but do not credit it as a cost saving; verify the real reason (parallelism, noisy output, independent review).
quote: Running out of context is rarely the problem anymore.

claim: The docs list as obsolete the habits of 'think hard' wording, 'keep going / don't be lazy' lines, and treating context as the main constraint to manage aggressively.
why: Effort is the control for thinking depth, and current models carry on through an agreed task.
check: Flag prompts and instruction files with these older-model workarounds.
quote: lines like that are more likely to cause over-work than fix a stall

claim: Phrases like think step by step are ordinary prompt text that only nudges within the effort setting; effort is the main control, and ultrathink asks for deeper reasoning for one turn.
why: The docs say wording cannot lift reasoning past the effort level.
check: Replace thinking-keyword prompts with /effort changes where depth matters.
quote: Those phrases are ordinary prompt text that nudges Claude within its effort setting rather than keywords that raise it.

claim: Effort defaults to medium on Fable 5.2, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5; the docs say raise it to high or xhigh for easily missed edge cases, lower it for quick iteration, and keep max for hard unattended problems because it tends to overthink ordinary tasks.
why: Higher effort spends more time and tokens for checking more cases.
check: Check pinned effortLevel or CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL; max as a global default is a cost finding.
quote: On ordinary tasks it tends to overthink, so you pay more for an answer that may be no better than `high` would have given you.

claim: Every request resends the whole conversation, so a session mixing unrelated tasks keeps paying for old history; /clear between unrelated tasks is free and is still recommended despite the 1M window.
why: Cache discounts apply only while warm, and a focused context also gives better answers.
check: Look at session habits and whether long sessions accumulate unrelated tasks.
quote: Every request sends the whole conversation, so a session that's collected three unrelated tasks re-reads all three on every turn of the fourth.

claim: The prompt cache lasts about an hour on a subscription and five minutes on an API key, cloud provider, or usage credits, and subagents get five minutes unless changed.
why: Cache expiry turns discounted reads into full-price input.
check: On API-key setups, consider ENABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_1H and check idle patterns.
quote: lasts about an hour on a subscription and five minutes on an API key, cloud provider, or usage credits.

claim: On Pro, Max, Ultra, Team and Enterprise, /usage breaks usage down by skill, subagent, plugin and MCP server and flags long context or frequent cache misses once one passes 10% of usage.
why: It is the docs' first stop for finding where tokens go.
check: Ask for /usage output before judging which extensions are worth their cost.
quote: It also flags patterns like long context or frequent cache misses once one of them passes 10% of your usage.

claim: The statusline command runs locally and does not consume API tokens, so a context and cost statusline is a free way to watch usage.
why: It reads JSON from stdin (cost.total_cost_usd, context_window.used_percentage) produced client-side.
check: Suggest a statusline showing context used_percentage; note cost is an estimate at list price that may differ from the bill.
quote: The status line runs locally and does not consume API tokens.

claim: The statusline cost.total_cost_usd field is an estimate computed client-side at list price (unless custom model pricing is configured) and resets to $0 on /clear, so it can differ from the actual bill.
why: It is an estimate, not billing data.
check: Do not use it as billing truth when judging a change's cost impact.
quote: Estimated session cost in USD, computed client-side at list price unless a

claim: Compaction summaries keep requests and key code but can lose detailed early instructions, so persistent rules belong in CLAUDE.md; a Compact Instructions section or /compact with a focus steers what is kept.
why: CLAUDE.md is reloaded; conversation history is summarized.
check: Check whether long-lived rules live only in prompts, and whether CLAUDE.md has Compact Instructions.
quote: The summary keeps your requests and key code snippets, but detailed instructions from early in the conversation may be lost.

claim: If one file or tool output is so large that context refills right after each summary, Claude Code stops auto-compacting after a few attempts and shows an error rather than looping.
why: It prevents a compaction loop.
check: Look for huge-output commands or reads that would trigger this.
quote: Claude Code stops auto-compacting after a few attempts and shows an error instead of looping.

claim: The first 200 lines or 25KB of auto memory's MEMORY.md, whichever comes first, load at session start.
why: Auto memory is an always-loaded surface with a hard cutoff.
check: If MEMORY.md exceeds this, content past the cutoff is not loaded at start.
quote: The first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md, whichever comes first, load at the start of each session.

claim: Claude Code adds its own context besides your files, including output-style instructions, commit and PR attribution lines and file-change notes, so a rule Claude follows may not come from the user's setup.
why: System reminders explain behaviors such as a Co-Authored-By trailer; attribution and includeGitInstructions settings control them.
check: Before blaming a CLAUDE.md for a behavior, check attribution and includeGitInstructions settings.
quote: the rule may have come from a

claim: Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md files from the working directory and every parent at launch and subdirectory files on demand; splitting per directory means only the relevant subsystem's conventions are in context.
why: One root file either grows to cover everything or stays generic.
check: In a large repo, check that subsystem conventions are not all in the root CLAUDE.md.
quote: Splitting instructions across per-directory files means Claude loads repository-wide rules plus only the conventions for the code you're working in.

claim: Starting from a subdirectory loads that directory's and every ancestor's CLAUDE.md and limits file access to that subtree, whereas starting at the repo root loads only the root file and loads subdirectory files on demand.
why: Launch directory sets access, memory loading, and which project settings apply.
check: Check where the user launches Claude relative to where the conventions live.
quote: Project settings in `.claude/settings.json` aren't inherited from parent directories the way CLAUDE.md files are.

claim: claudeMdExcludes skips CLAUDE.md and rules for packages you never work in; the list is static, so for per-task focus start Claude from that package's directory instead.
why: Exclusions are not a per-task switch.
check: Check for claudeMdExcludes in shared settings that are really personal and belong in settings.local.json.
quote: The exclusion list is static, not a per-task switch.

claim: Review CLAUDE.md after major model releases and delete workarounds for old model limitations, since they become overhead once a newer model handles the case.
why: Instructions written for older models can be dead weight.
check: Look for rules compensating for limitations of earlier models; /doctor prompt-audit can flag them.
quote: instructions that worked around an older model's limitation may become overhead once a newer model handles the case on its own

claim: Search respects .gitignore by default, so gitignored build output needs no config; checked-in vendored or generated code needs Read deny rules, which do not cover subprocesses that open files themselves.
why: Deny rules only catch built-in tools and recognized file commands.
check: Look for checked-in generated or vendored directories that Claude reads wastefully.
quote: Deny rules don't cover subprocesses that open files themselves.

claim: Directories added through the additionalDirectories setting grant file access only and never load CLAUDE.md, rules or skills; --add-dir loads skills but needs CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD=1 for memory files.
why: The two mechanisms differ in what they load.
check: If a setup expects a sibling package's conventions to load via additionalDirectories, it will not.
quote: The environment variable has no effect on directories listed in the `additionalDirectories` setting.

claim: Claude chooses among skills by reading every discovered name and description and loads only the chosen skill's content; with many skills some lose their descriptions, so descriptions should be short and lead with words a request would contain.
why: Starting from the repo root accumulates skills from every touched subdirectory, possibly hundreds.
check: Count skills in scope and check description length and keywords.
quote: Claude picks a skill by reading every discovered skill's name and description, and only the chosen skill's full content loads into context.

claim: Team procedures (release process, runbooks, doc style) belong in skills rather than CLAUDE.md, with disable-model-invocation for side-effect workflows, because a long procedure in a skill does not weigh on unrelated tasks.
why: Only name and description load every session; the body loads when needed.
check: Flag multi-step procedures stored in CLAUDE.md.
quote: A long release procedure sitting in a skill doesn't weigh on your unrelated bug fix the way it would in `CLAUDE.md`.

claim: A skill must be a folder with SKILL.md (.claude/skills/name/SKILL.md); a bare .claude/skills/name.md does not appear in /skills.
why: The debug table lists this as a common cause of missing skills.
check: Check skill file layout.
quote: Use a folder with `SKILL.md` inside: `.claude/skills/name/SKILL.md`.

claim: The commands/*.md directory is the same mechanism as skills, as single-file prompts.
why: Commands are not a separate extension point; skills are the current form.
check: Treat legacy commands as skills when auditing; migration to skills/ is optional.
quote: Single-file prompts; same mechanism as skills

claim: /skill-doctor shows what each skill costs in context and how often it is used so unused skills can be turned off, and /skills can sort by token count.
why: They are the built-in inspection tools for skill overhead.
check: Use them, or the OTel skill_activated event, to find skills that cost context but never run.
quote: costs in context and how often it gets used

claim: Skill usage can be measured with the OpenTelemetry logs exporter and OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1, which records skill names verbatim; the skill_activated event shows who invoked each skill.
why: It identifies skills to consolidate or retire.
check: If a team asks which skills pay off, point to this telemetry.
quote: set `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS=1` so skill names are recorded verbatim instead of redacted

claim: Hooks belong under the hooks key of settings.json; there is no standalone hooks file for project or user config, and only plugins load a separate hooks/hooks.json.
why: A hook in a standalone file never loads.
check: Verify hooks are in settings.json (or a plugin), and matcher is a single string using | not an array.
quote: There is no standalone hooks file for project or user config.

claim: Hook matchers are case-sensitive and use capitalized tool names (Bash, Edit, Write, Read); a misspelled name matches nothing so the hook fails silently, and an array matcher is invalid.
why: A hook that never fires gives no error.
check: Check matchers for lowercase tool names, arrays, and comma separators on versions before v2.1.191.
quote: Matching is case-sensitive. Tool names are capitalized: `Bash`, `Edit`, `Write`, `Read`.

claim: Project MCP config goes in .mcp.json at the repo root with servers under mcpServers; settings.json does not read an mcpServers key, and a file inside .claude/ is not read.
why: Misplaced MCP config silently never loads.
check: Check .mcp.json location, key name, and whether the one-time project-server approval was dismissed.
quote: Project MCP config goes at the repository root as `.mcp.json`, not inside `.claude/`, with servers under the `mcpServers` key.

claim: Connected MCP servers add tool names and instructions to context even when unused, tool search defers full schemas by default, and unneeded servers should be disabled.
why: Idle servers cost context; ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=auto defers once definitions reach 10% of the window.
check: Run /mcp and /context all; many servers with large tool lists, or tool search disabled, is a finding.
quote: `auto` turns tool search on once definitions reach 10% of the context window.

claim: Settings merge managed first, then local over project over user; command-line flags and environment variables are an additional override layer, so a seemingly ignored setting is usually overridden elsewhere.
why: The debug guide names override by another scope or env var as the usual cause.
check: When a setting does not apply, check settings.local.json, flags, env vars, and /status for managed settings.
quote: Managed settings apply first when present. Among the rest, the closer scope overrides the broader one in the order local, then project, then user.

claim: ~/.claude.json holds app state and UI toggles; permissions, hooks and env belong in ~/.claude/settings.json, which are two different files.
why: Putting config in the wrong file means it is ignored.
check: Look for hooks or permissions in ~/.claude.json.
quote: `~/.claude.json` holds app state and UI toggles.

claim: Project .claude/settings.json is not inherited from parent directories, and inside a worktree the session loads the worktree root's copy, so deny rules needed there must be in the repo root settings.
why: Per-area settings files must be self-contained.
check: In monorepos, verify deny rules and hooks exist where worktree and subdirectory sessions will read them.
quote: Each subdirectory's `.claude/settings.json` must be self-contained rather than layered on a root file.

claim: The .claude directory layout: CLAUDE.md, rules/*.md, settings.json, settings.local.json, skills/<name>/SKILL.md, commands/*.md, output-styles/*.md, agents/*.md, workflows/*.js, agent-memory/; .mcp.json and .worktreeinclude sit at the repo root; ~/.claude.json, keybindings and auto memory are global only.
why: Each kind of customization has one home, listed in the docs' file reference.
check: Flag config in the wrong file (e.g. agents in settings.json, MCP in .claude/).
quote: Different kinds of customization live in different files. Use this table to find where a change belongs.

claim: Personal project preferences go in CLAUDE.local.md (gitignored) and personal settings in settings.local.json; Claude Code adds settings.local.json to gitignore only when it saves a setting there.
why: Shared files should hold only team-wide content.
check: Check that personal preferences are not committed in CLAUDE.md or settings.json and that hand-made local files are gitignored.
quote: Your personal preferences go in `CLAUDE.local.md` instead of `CLAUDE.md`, and you add that file to `.gitignore` so it stays out of the repo.

claim: Managed settings override every settings file and --settings value apart from narrow exceptions, making them the only place for organization policy.
why: No personal file can override them.
check: Security policy placed in user or project settings is not enforceable; check /status for managed sources.
quote: Enterprise-enforced settings that your own settings files and `--settings` values can't override

claim: Transcripts, which can include file contents, command output, pasted secrets, and the loaded instruction files, are stored unencrypted under ~/.claude/projects and deleted after cleanupPeriodDays (default 30, minimum 1).
why: Anything passing through a tool is written to disk.
check: For sensitive repos, check cleanupPeriodDays, deny rules on credential files, and CLAUDE_CODE_SKIP_PROMPT_HISTORY.
quote: Transcripts and history are not encrypted at rest.

claim: Claude Code snapshots files before edits as checkpoints for the 100 most recent prompts in a session, kept with the conversation, and /rewind (alias /undo, or Esc twice) restores code, conversation, or both.
why: Snapshots are deleted by the retention sweep after about 30 days.
check: Check cleanupPeriodDays if long-lived rewind is expected.
quote: Claude Code keeps file snapshots for the 100 most recent checkpoints in a session.

claim: Checkpoints do not track files changed only by Bash commands, most subagent edits, external edits or other sessions, nor symlinked and hard-linked files, and are not a replacement for git.
why: Only edits through Claude's file tools in the main conversation are captured.
check: Do not treat checkpointing as safety for Bash-driven or subagent-driven changes; check that git commits are used.
quote: A file that only Bash commands changed isn't tracked and stays as it is.

claim: Resuming a session reopens it with the same session ID and appends to it, while forking (/branch or --fork-session) copies history to a new ID; resuming one session in two terminals makes both write to one transcript and can lose messages.
why: Use --fork-session to keep both conversations.
check: Check parallel-work habits for concurrent resumes of the same session.
quote: If you resume the same session in two terminals or two `claude -p` runs at the same time, both write to one transcript.

claim: On resume Claude Code does not restore --mcp-config, --plugin-dir, --add-dir, --settings or --fallback-model, which must be passed again.
why: Those launch flags are not saved with the session.
check: Scripts that resume sessions should repeat these flags.
quote: because Claude Code doesn't restore them

claim: The session transcript entry format is internal and changes between versions, so scripts should use /export, claude -p --output-format json, hooks' transcript_path, or the Agent SDK instead of parsing the JSONL.
why: Direct parsing can break on any release.
check: Flag tooling that parses ~/.claude/projects JSONL directly.
quote: The entry format is internal to Claude Code and changes between versions, so scripts that parse these files directly can break on any release.

claim: After two failed corrections the docs recommend /clear plus one better prompt instead of a third correction, and Esc or /rewind to steer early.
why: A third correction adds to a conversation that already contains two failed attempts.
check: Check how users recover from drift.
quote: after two failed corrections run `/clear` and write a better prompt instead of a third.

claim: /context shows everything occupying the context window by category (system prompt, tools, MCP tools, subagents, memory files, skills, messages); subdirectory CLAUDE.md files load on demand and so do not appear there at session start.
why: It is the first step to confirm a CLAUDE.md, rule or skill description is present at all.
check: Run /context all before diagnosing an ignored instruction.
quote: The `/context` command shows everything occupying the context window for the current session.

claim: Inspection commands: /memory (memory files), /skills, /hooks, /mcp, /permissions (resolved rules), /doctor (setup checkup), /debug, /status (active settings sources including managed).
why: Each shows what loaded for one category.
check: Use them to verify a configuration before concluding it is correct; claude doctor prints diagnostics without a session.
quote: Active settings sources, including whether managed settings are in effect

claim: /doctor checks installation, invalid settings, unused extensions, duplicate subagent names and CLAUDE.md content derivable from code, and /doctor prompt-audit flags instructions written for older models, dead file references and contradictions.
why: They are built-in audits of instruction files.
check: Run them or reproduce their checks when auditing.
quote: `/doctor prompt-audit` flags instructions that were written for older models, point at files that no longer exist, or

claim: To isolate a config problem, run claude --safe-mode, which disables CLAUDE.md, skills, plugins, hooks, MCP servers, commands, agents, styles and keybindings while keeping auth, model, built-in tools and permissions.
why: If the problem disappears, the cause is among the disabled items.
check: Use safe mode first; if it persists, use a clean CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR with --setting-sources user.
quote: Authentication, model selection, built-in tools, and permissions work normally.

claim: CLAUDE.md adherence drops when instructions are vague, when two files conflict, or when the file is so long that individual rules get less attention; CLAUDE.md is guidance while permissions and hooks enforce limits.
why: If /context shows the file loaded and Claude still ignores a line, the cause is how the instruction is written.
check: After confirming load, review ambiguity, conflicts, and length.
quote: Adherence drops when an instruction is vague enough to interpret multiple ways, when two files give conflicting direction, or when the file has grown long enough that individual rules get less attention.

claim: The --bare flag for scripted runs skips hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers and CLAUDE.md, and hooks passed with --settings do not run under it.
why: It makes runs reproducible across machines.
check: CI scripts that depend on repo instructions or hooks must not use --bare.
quote: skips hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, and `CLAUDE.md` files, the repo's as well as the machine's

claim: @ file references include file contents without a tool call, so PreToolUse hooks do not run for them; use Read deny rules or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FILE_MENTIONS=1.
why: Hook-based read controls are bypassed by @ includes.
check: If a setup relies on a PreToolUse hook to control reads, check the @ gap.
quote: don't run when Claude Code includes a file you reference with `@`, because it makes no tool call.

claim: Code Mode is experimental and off by default, lets Claude write JavaScript making several tool calls, and in auto mode the classifier reviews the code not each tool call, so deny/ask rules and PreToolUse hooks still apply per call.
why: The classifier cannot see run-time computed values.
check: If Code Mode is on, keep rules or hooks for calls that must be controlled.
quote: the classifier reviews each piece of code before it runs, not each tool call.

claim: CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE can only lower the auto-compact trigger (e.g. 50 to compact earlier), and CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW sets the window between 100000 and 1000000 tokens.
why: Both control how full context gets before compaction.
check: Check whether compaction tuning matches long-session cost goals.
quote: Use lower values like `50` to compact earlier; the variable can't raise the threshold, so values above the default percentage are ignored.

claim: CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT holds 1M-window models to 200K, and CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_CLAUDE_MDS stops loading any CLAUDE.md including user, project and auto memory files.
why: They change how much context is available or loaded.
check: An unexpected 200K window or missing memory may trace to these variables.
quote: Claude Code removes `[1m]` model variants from the model picker and holds models that run with the 1M window by default to a 200K window.

claim: Models Fable, Sonnet 5 and later, Haiku 5.5 and Opus 4.7 and later always use adaptive reasoning, so disabling adaptive thinking applies only to Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6; MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=0 disables thinking explicitly.
why: Fixed thinking budgets do not apply to current models.
check: Flag MAX_THINKING_TOKENS or DISABLE_ADAPTIVE_THINKING settings on current models as likely no-ops.
quote: or Opus 4.7 and later, which always use adaptive reasoning

claim: CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL takes precedence over --effort, /effort and the effortLevel settings, so a forgotten env var can silently pin effort.
why: It is the top of the effort precedence chain, still subject to maxEffortLevel.
check: Check the shell and settings env block for it when effort seems stuck.
quote: Takes precedence over `--effort`, `/effort`, and the `modelSettings` and `effortLevel` settings.

claim: CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1 forces one model onto subagents, teammates and workflow agents, overriding per-agent model choices.
why: It overrides model: haiku settings in agent definitions.
check: If subagents run on an expensive model despite model: haiku, check this variable.
quote: Set to `1` to force one model onto subagents, teammates, and workflow agents.

claim: MCP tool responses are capped at 25000 tokens by default with a warning above 10,000, file reads at 25,000 tokens, and bash output at 30000 characters (max 150000).
why: These limits bound how much a single tool result adds to context.
check: Raised limits (MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS, BASH_MAX_OUTPUT_LENGTH) add context cost per call; check why they were raised.
quote: Maximum number of tokens allowed in MCP tool responses (default: 25000).

claim: CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE=1 runs a minimal system prompt with only Bash, read and edit tools and disables auto-discovery of hooks, skills, subagents, plugins, MCP, auto memory and CLAUDE.md.
why: It is a stripped-down baseline.
check: A useful no-configuration baseline when measuring whether a setup changes outcomes.
quote: Set to `1` to run with a minimal system prompt and only the Bash, file read, and file edit tools.

claim: Before leaving a run unattended, the docs ask five questions: does it know what done looks like, can it check its own work, what may it touch, what stops it (--max-turns, --max-budget-usd), and who signs off.
why: Without a person watching, a wrong assumption compounds all night.
check: For scheduled or headless setups, confirm each answer exists.
quote: Before a run goes unattended, make sure it knows what done looks like, can check its own work, and can only touch what it should.

claim: /simplify reviews changed code for cleanup but not correctness bugs, while /code-review looks for correctness bugs, with fresh-subagent independence.
why: The two review commands have different scope.
check: Do not substitute one for the other in a review workflow.
quote: The review doesn't look for correctness bugs. Use `/code-review` to find bugs.

claim: /init generates a starter CLAUDE.md, and CLAUDE_CODE_NEW_INIT=1 makes it an interactive flow that also covers skills, hooks and personal memory files; the docs say the work after /init is mostly removing lines.
why: Generated files tend to include content Claude can derive from code.
check: Check whether an init-generated CLAUDE.md was pruned.
quote: Set `CLAUDE_CODE_NEW_INIT=1` for an interactive flow that also walks through skills, hooks, and personal memory files.

claim: The engineering-blog snapshot of Claude Code best practices is word-for-word identical to the current best-practices doc, so it shows no older/newer disagreement.
why: The snapshot supplied under the engineering post's name has the current page's content, including 'What you can stop doing'.
check: Do not cite the engineering snapshot as older guidance; it carries the current recommendations.
quote: Every one of these was good advice when it was written.

claim: Audit an eval before trusting it, since the most surprising eval results usually turn out to be bugs in the eval rather than facts about the model.
why: A broken eval produces confident numbers pointing the wrong way, and hillclimbing on it multiplies the error.
check: Before accepting a before/after comparison, ask whether the eval itself was audited and run end to end.
quote: In practice the most surprising eval results usually turn out to be bugs in the eval rather than facts about the model

claim: Test the harness with an oracle that should pass and a null baseline that should fail before any full pass.
why: If the oracle fails the harness or grader is broken, and if the null passes the grader is too lenient.
check: Look for evidence both checks were run; absence is a finding.
quote: If the oracle doesn't pass, the harness or grader is broken; if the null doesn't fail, the grader is too lenient.

claim: Never use one model's outputs as gold when comparing that model with another; reference-match scoring then rewards imitating the incumbent.
why: Gold from the incumbent makes it look best by construction.
check: For model or config migrations, ask where the expected outputs came from and prefer rubric or pairwise judging.
quote: Never use model A's outputs as gold when the question is A vs B.

claim: Keep infra failures, truncations and refusals out of the model-failure column; a timeout, rate-limit error, or response cut at max_tokens scored as 0 contaminates the headline.
why: Non-model artifacts get attributed to the model when conflated.
check: Check how the runner handles errors and whether truncated and refused rows are labeled separately.
quote: any time a non-model artifact - an infra error, a truncated response, a broken tool, a retry delay - lands in the same column as a genuine model result

claim: The grader must distinguish a model asserting a negative from a model failing to produce an answer.
why: Otherwise a runner that errors on every input scores like one that carefully found nothing.
check: In detection or classification evals, confirm empty or crashed outputs do not map to the 'none' label.
quote: If both land on the same label, a runner that errors on every input scores identically to one that carefully found nothing.

claim: Run multiple trials and report intervals; differences smaller than run-to-run spread are not meaningful, and for a pass rate the noise floor is roughly 1/sqrt(n*R), about plus or minus 14 points at 25 cases and 2 reps.
why: A single rep is a point estimate with no error bar.
check: If a claimed improvement is smaller than the noise floor at the actual case and rep count, it is not evidence.
quote: for a pass-rate, roughly `1/sqrt(n·R)`: 25 cases × 2 reps ~ ±14 points, 100 × 2 ~ ±7

claim: The eval config must match production: the runner should call the app's real entry point with the same system prompt, tools, model and sampling.
why: A re-implemented call measures a different setup.
check: Diff the eval's setup against the shipped configuration (including CLAUDE.md, skills and hooks for Claude Code evals).
quote: The runner must call the app's real entry point; a re-implemented call silently measures a different setup.

claim: For agents that act on an environment, grade the end state (tests pass, diff applies, files present) rather than the transcript, adding a judge only for taste dimensions.
why: A judge reading a coding transcript is grading the narration.
check: Check whether agentic evals inspect the workspace outcome.
quote: A judge reading a coding transcript is grading the narration; the environment is the answer.

claim: Graders should score outcomes, not paths, so a model that solves the task a different valid way is not failed for tool order or phrasing.
why: Path grading penalizes valid solutions.
check: Look for graders that require exact tool-call sequences.
quote: Requiring an exact tool-call sequence, phrasing, or intermediate step fails a model that solved it a different valid way.

claim: Draw train/test splits at random (stratified by tag), never by baseline score, because a train set of worst cases gains from regression to the mean while held-out stays flat.
why: Selecting low scorers makes cases 'improve' on re-run by chance.
check: Check how the split was made and whether train and test baselines agree within noise.
quote: the split must be drawn at random (stratified by `tags[0]`), never by baseline score.

claim: Confirm the mechanism under test is wired: disable the instruction file, tool or memory and confirm the score drops, and confirm it engages in transcripts.
why: If the score barely moves either way the eval is not measuring the lever.
check: For an eval of a CLAUDE.md or skill change, check for an ablation run and transcripts showing the skill or file used.
quote: disable it and confirm the score drops; enable it and confirm it engages in the transcripts.

claim: An LLM judge needs a randomized A/B order, no reward for length, a different family than the model under test, a concrete rubric, and calibration against human labels (well below about 90% agreement on clear cases means iterate).
why: Judges show position, verbosity and self-preference bias.
check: Check a judge-graded eval for these controls and a human-agreement number.
quote: A judge from the same family as a model under test tends to prefer outputs that resemble its own

claim: Spot-check outputs the grader marked wrong; if more than roughly one in ten look like grader errors, fix the grader before any full pass.
why: Otherwise you are measuring which variant matches the grader's blind spots.
check: Ask whether failures were read by a person.
quote: If more than roughly one in ten look like grader errors, fix the grader before any full pass

claim: Check headroom: with a baseline near 95% or above the eval cannot discriminate at the top, and a 0% result is more often a broken case or grader than a hard task.
why: Saturated or floored evals do not show improvement.
check: Compute baseline score against the effect size sought.
quote: If the baseline already scores ~95%+, the eval cannot discriminate at the top

claim: Cover both directions of a behavior (search when needed and not when unneeded), or one-sided evals produce one-sided optimization.
why: An always-search policy would score perfectly on a one-sided eval.
check: For tool-use, refusal or escalation evals, confirm negative cases exist.
quote: otherwise always-search scores perfectly and one-sided evals produce one-sided optimisation

claim: Take token counts from the API usage block, record cost from recorded tokens and the actual model including cache rates, and time only the final successful request for latency.
why: Estimates can reverse a cost comparison, and retries make one variant look slower.
check: Check cost and latency columns for estimated tokens, flat rates, or retry time included.
quote: String-length estimates are off by enough to reverse a cost comparison.

claim: Verify the served model matches the requested model on every call and save full per-case trajectories so a surprising score can be traced to the model or the eval.
why: A score served by the wrong model measures nothing.
check: Look for a model assertion on responses and saved transcripts.
quote: A score served by the wrong model measures nothing

claim: Anthropic's API docs say to define success criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, and to use multidimensional criteria rather than one vague goal.
why: Vague criteria like 'performs well' cannot be tested.
check: Check whether a change's goal is stated with a metric, threshold and test population.
quote: Most use cases need multidimensional evaluation along several success criteria.

claim: The API docs say to prefer volume over per-item quality: many automatically graded questions beat fewer hand-graded ones.
why: Bd-eval-audit stresses label correctness and case quality, so the sources differ in emphasis; the docs here optimize for automation and coverage.
check: Weigh both: a large auto-graded set still needs label and grader verification.
quote: More questions with slightly lower signal automated grading is better than fewer questions with high-quality human hand-graded evals.

claim: Grade by code first (fastest and most reliable), use LLM grading when judgment is needed after testing its reliability, and avoid human grading where possible; LLM graders need clear rubrics.
why: The docs rank methods by speed, reliability and scalability.
check: Check that deterministic checks are used wherever the property can be checked in code.
quote: Most flexible and high quality, but slow and expensive. Avoid if possible.

claim: Design evals to mirror the real task distribution including edge cases such as irrelevant input, overly long input and ambiguous cases.
why: Evals unlike production traffic do not predict production results.
check: Compare eval cases with real usage in the repo or sessions.
quote: Design evals that mirror your real-world task distribution.
